prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from being cured when the rash faded, the patient still carried a ------- form of the virus that could reawaken in her nerve cells decades later.
explanation: 'Far from being cured' and 'could reawaken ... decades later' mean the virus is present but hidden and inactive: latent.
distractor_rationales: nascent — nascent means just beginning to develop; the virus is not new but lying dormant until it 'reawakens'.
manifest — manifest means plainly visible; the rash had faded, so nothing was visible.
jaundiced — jaundiced describes yellowed skin or a bitter outlook, not a virus hiding in nerve cells.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The new battery's capacity sounds impressive in the advertisement, but its gains over last year's model are merely -------, a two-percent improvement at best.
explanation: 'Sounds impressive ... but merely' and 'a two-percent improvement' call for a word meaning small, step-by-step gains: incremental.
distractor_rationales: monumental — monumental means huge, the opposite of 'merely' a two-percent gain.
hypothetical — the two-percent improvement is measured and real, so the gains are not hypothetical.
pivotal — pivotal means decisive; 'merely' and 'two percent at best' deny that the gains matter much.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Glaciologists had assumed the ice shelf would retreat over centuries, yet the satellite record shows a ------- collapse: ice that had stood for millennia disintegrated within a single summer.
explanation: 'Yet' reverses 'over centuries'; 'disintegrated within a single summer' means the collapse was sudden and rushing: headlong.
distractor_rationales: protracted — protracted means drawn out, which is what the scientists assumed, not what the record shows.
periodic — periodic means recurring at intervals; this was a single unprecedented event.
glacial — glacial means extremely slow, the expectation that 'yet' overturns.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the compound dissolves instantly in alcohol, it is ------- in water, so the researchers had to abandon their plan to give it to patients as a simple drinking solution.
explanation: 'Although it dissolves instantly in alcohol' sets up the opposite behavior in water, and the abandoned drinking solution confirms it will not dissolve: insoluble.
distractor_rationales: gaseous — gaseous describes a state of matter, not how a compound behaves when mixed into water; it would not explain the failed solution.
inert — inert means it does not react; a nonreactive compound could still be dissolved and drunk, so the plan would not have to be abandoned.
potable — potable means safe to drink, which would make a drinking solution easier, not impossible.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The physician warned that the drug's side effects were -------: they crept in so gradually over many months that most patients never connected their growing fatigue to the medication.
explanation: Harm that 'crept in so gradually' that patients 'never connected' it to the drug is harm that advances unnoticed: insidious.
distractor_rationales: patent — patent means plainly evident; these effects went unnoticed.
lurid — lurid means vivid and shocking; a slowly growing fatigue is neither.
hyperbolic — hyperbolic means exaggerated; the warning is that the effects are real but hidden, not overstated.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Most metals crack when struck again and again, but gold is so ------- that a single ounce can be hammered into a sheet large enough to cover a small room.
explanation: 'But' contrasts gold with metals that crack under hammering; being beaten into a huge thin sheet shows it can be shaped without breaking: malleable.
distractor_rationales: granular — granular means made of grains, which would make the metal crumble, not spread into a sheet.
opalescent — opalescent describes a milky shimmer of color and says nothing about surviving hammering.
hermetic — hermetic means airtight; it has nothing to do with being beaten thin.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Whereas the finished robot had a single button that a child could operate, the first prototype was so ------- that even its own builders needed a thick manual just to switch it on.
explanation: 'Whereas' contrasts the one-button final design; needing a thick manual just to switch it on means the prototype was bewilderingly complicated: labyrinthine.
distractor_rationales: minimalist — minimalist describes the one-button final design, the very thing 'whereas' contrasts with the prototype.
monolithic — monolithic means a single uniform block, which would be simple, not something requiring a manual.
gossamer — gossamer means light and delicate; it does not explain why the machine was hard to operate.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the comet looks ------- to the naked eye, a faint smudge easily mistaken for a distant star, a telescope reveals a glowing tail that stretches millions of kilometers.
explanation: 'Although' sets the naked-eye view against the spectacular telescope view; 'a faint smudge easily mistaken for a distant star' means it looks unremarkable: nondescript.
distractor_rationales: gargantuan — gargantuan means enormous, which is what the telescope reveals, not what the naked eye sees.
kaleidoscopic — kaleidoscopic means brightly multicolored and changing; a faint smudge is neither.
incandescent — incandescent means glowing brilliantly, the opposite of a faint smudge.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The programmer's patch proved merely -------: the crashes stopped for a week, but because the memory leak causing them was never found, they returned as soon as traffic doubled.
explanation: A fix that quiets the symptom (the crashes) for a while without curing the cause (the leak) is palliative.
distractor_rationales: pernicious — pernicious means harmful; the patch did not cause damage, it stopped the crashes for a week.
holistic — holistic means treating the whole system; this patch ignored the underlying leak.
orthodox — orthodox means conventional; nothing in the sentence concerns whether the method was standard, and 'merely' plus the returning crashes point to a temporary fix.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Rather than giving every patient the same dose, the clinic now tailors treatment to each person's genes, having learned that people's responses to the drug are strikingly -------.
explanation: Dropping one dose for all ('rather than') in favor of tailoring only makes sense if responses differ widely from person to person: heterogeneous.
distractor_rationales: invariable — invariable means unchanging and uniform, which would justify one dose for everyone, the policy the clinic dropped.
gradual — gradual describes the speed of a response, not why each patient needs a different dose.
optimal — optimal means already ideal, which would give no reason to change the dosing.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Many desert shrubs look dead through the long dry season, yet they are anything but -------; within hours of the first rain they unfurl bright new leaves.
explanation: 'Look dead ... yet anything but' calls for a word meaning near death, which the quick new leaves disprove: moribund.
distractor_rationales: gnarled — gnarled means twisted and knotted; the shrubs may well be gnarled, and leafing out does not disprove it.
noxious — noxious means harmful or poisonous; the sentence is about seeming dead versus being alive.
germinal — germinal means in an early stage of growth; 'anything but' must deny the look of death, not of newness.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Though the herbal tonic was once sold as a cure for nearly every ailment, careful trials showed it to be -------, doing no more for patients than a sugar pill.
explanation: 'Though ... a cure for nearly every ailment' is reversed by 'no more than a sugar pill': the tonic has no real effect, ineffectual.
distractor_rationales: poisonous — poisonous means toxic, but a sugar pill does no harm; the comparison is about doing nothing.
palatable — palatable means pleasant to taste, which the trials of effectiveness did not address.
miraculous — miraculous is the claim the trials overturned.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Doctors long regarded damage to heart muscle as -------, but new research shows that heart cells can slowly regenerate after an attack.
explanation: 'But' sets the old view against the finding that cells 'can slowly regenerate'; the old view must have been that the damage could never be undone: irreversible.
distractor_rationales: gratuitous — gratuitous means uncalled-for; regeneration does not answer whether damage was necessary.
pervasive — pervasive means widespread; regrowth of cells does not contradict how far damage spreads.
illusory — illusory would mean the damage was not real, but regeneration presupposes real damage, so 'but' would make no sense.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Critics dismissed the early internet as a ------- curiosity, never guessing that within two decades it would reshape how nearly everyone shops, works, and talks.
explanation: 'Dismissed' plus 'never guessing it would reshape how nearly everyone' lives means critics saw it as something of interest only to a small group: niche.
distractor_rationales: groundbreaking — groundbreaking is praise, not a dismissal, and is what critics failed to foresee.
nefarious — nefarious means wicked; the critics' mistake was about how widely it would matter, not about morality.
menacing — menacing means threatening; 'curiosity' and 'never guessing' its reach point to unimportance, not danger.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Parents often treat a high fever as the most alarming symptom, but the pediatrician explained that a fever is usually -------, a sign that the body is fighting the infection rather than losing to it.
explanation: 'But' reverses 'most alarming'; a fever that shows the body 'fighting the infection' is serving as a defense: protective.
distractor_rationales: hallucinatory — hallucinatory describes visions; it is not what shows the body fighting infection.
malignant — malignant means dangerous and spreading, which repeats the alarm 'but' overturns.
omnipresent — omnipresent means present everywhere; the sentence explains what a fever does, not how common it is.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although its maker boasted of the robot vacuum's intelligence, its navigation was -------: it bumped the same chair leg dozens of times before finding the doorway by chance.
explanation: 'Although ... intelligence' is reversed by repeated bumping and finding the door only 'by chance': the navigation was clumsy and unskilled, inept.
distractor_rationales: masterful — masterful repeats the maker's boast, which 'although' overturns.
lyrical — lyrical means expressive like poetry; it says nothing about skill at navigating.
officious — officious means meddling and bossy; the vacuum's failure is incompetence, not interference.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Unlike the dry valley below, the mountain's windward slope is so ------- that moss coats every boulder and ferns sprout from the trunks of the trees.
explanation: 'Unlike the dry valley' plus moss on every boulder and ferns on trunks describe thick, rich plant growth: lush.
distractor_rationales: gaunt — gaunt means bare and bleak, closer to the dry valley the slope is contrasted with.
jagged — jagged describes a rough outline, which would not cause moss and ferns to cover everything.
molten — molten means melted by heat; nothing can grow on molten rock.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Engineers called the bridge's new sensors -------, since they had flagged a hairline crack months before it grew large enough for any inspector to see.
explanation: Detecting a crack 'months before' anyone could see it is perceiving a problem ahead of time: prescient.
distractor_rationales: myopic — myopic means shortsighted, the opposite of catching a problem months early.
obtrusive — obtrusive means getting in the way; the sentence is praise for early detection.
histrionic — histrionic means overly dramatic; quietly flagging a hairline crack is the opposite of a theatrical display.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Most of the island's birds scattered when the sailors landed, but the dodo, having never met a predator, was dangerously -------, waddling right up to the men who would hunt it.
explanation: 'But' sets the dodo against the birds that fled; never having met a predator, it paid no attention to danger: heedless.
distractor_rationales: gangly — gangly means awkwardly tall and thin; build does not explain walking up to hunters.
lugubrious — lugubrious means mournful; the dodo's problem was lack of fear, not sadness.
overwrought — overwrought means agitated and nervous, the reaction of the birds that fled, not of the dodo.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Before the printing press, copying a book was so ------- that a single monk might labor for a year to produce one Bible by hand.
explanation: A year of one monk's labor for one book means the work was a heavy burden: onerous.
distractor_rationales: nominal — nominal means trivial in amount, the opposite of a year of labor.
mechanized — mechanized contradicts 'by hand'.
immaterial — immaterial means unimportant; the sentence stresses how much effort copying took.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Physicists had expected the new particle to be -------, decaying within a billionth of a second, but it survived long enough to cross the entire detector.
explanation: The expectation of 'decaying within a billionth of a second', reversed by 'but it survived', is of a very brief existence: momentary.
distractor_rationales: kinetic — kinetic means relating to motion; crossing the detector is the surprise, so it cannot be what was expected.
paradoxical — paradoxical means self-contradictory; nothing was expected to be contradictory, only short-lived.
orbital — orbital means circling something; the expectation concerned how long the particle would last.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The patient insisted his cough was -------, nothing worse than the tail end of a cold, but the X-ray revealed pneumonia.
explanation: 'Nothing worse than the tail end of a cold', reversed by the pneumonia finding, means he thought it unimportant: inconsequential.
distractor_rationales: incurable — incurable is the opposite of dismissing it as a lingering cold.
gastric — gastric refers to the stomach; a cough is not a stomach complaint.
melodious — melodious means pleasant-sounding; the contrast is about how serious the cough was.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The early search engine's results were so ------- that a query about jaguars returned pages on cars, cats, and football teams alike, whereas modern engines guess which meaning the user intends.
explanation: Returning every kind of 'jaguar' page alike, contrasted with engines that 'guess which meaning the user intends', means the results failed to make distinctions: indiscriminate.
distractor_rationales: pertinent — pertinent means relevant, which pages about the wrong jaguars were not.
parochial — parochial means narrow and limited, the opposite of results ranging over cars, cats, and football.
imperious — imperious means domineering; it describes a manner, not a set of search results.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Cars of the 1950s were ------- with fuel, burning a gallon every ten miles, whereas today's hybrids stretch the same gallon across fifty.
explanation: Burning a gallon every ten miles, set against hybrids that 'stretch' a gallon, means the old cars spent fuel wastefully: prodigal.
distractor_rationales: provident — provident means careful to save for the future, which describes the hybrids, not the gas-guzzlers.
glutted — glutted means overfilled; the sentence is about how fast fuel was used, not how full the tank was.
imbued — imbued means filled or soaked with a quality; it does not describe using fuel up quickly.
